title: Six ways in which technology can help learning happen
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton offers a measured case for six ways technology helps learning in schools, drawing on his own Duolingo practice and on school experience. Technology packages the repeated experiences that make knowledge stick, though it cannot coach a learner through a skills breakdown. It gives rapid feedback, as with a reading programme he saw in use. It must also be engaging, and he describes a maths programme teachers praised while students and parents found it demotivating. Further, it is always on, can improve local evidence through data analysis, and can support parent engagement if teacher messaging is not overdone. He promises a follow-up on how technology gets in the way.
points: Technology is well suited to delivering the intensive repeated experiences that make knowledge sticky, but it falls short at the point of skills breakdown, where human coaching is needed.
Instant feedback and tracking of errors, as in a school reading programme, can free the teacher to help the pupils who still struggle.
Efficiency is not enough: school programmes compete with the commercial technology children use elsewhere, and a dull but orderly maths programme left students and parents unmotivated.
Simple data analysis can show which lessons produce learning, who teaches them and which students seldom learn, supporting evidence-based decisions.
Parent communication tools can help partnership but risk overload for teachers and families when used too often.
quotes: Technology is an ideal vehicle to package and deliver the repeated experiences necessary to make knowledge sticky. School classrooms and busy homes are not places that make it easy for children and students to repeatedly experience the facts that we think are important. There is too much going on and too much interference. But creating age-appropriate programs into which the required knowledge can be entered and then experienced repeatedly by students seems to be simple technology at its best.

How do I get coached to overcome the problem I am having? You Tube is good at showing me what something looks like. It is good at getting me started. It is good at enabling me to watch the lesson repeatedly. But at breakdown, I need coaching which will usually require a real person who can assess where and how the breakdown happened and how I am responding to the breakdown.

If technology is to really help learning happen in schools, it has to be engaging as well as efficient. If it can’t be engaging as well as efficient it will simply end up as a modern equivalent of the classroom in Charles Dickens’ Hard Times, where Mr Gradgrind continually asked the 50 sullen students knowledge questions such as: ‘What’s the Definition of a Horse?

Classrooms aren’t always on. In fact, most classrooms turn themselves on and off every 40 minutes or so. If I haven’t quite had enough repeated experience as the lesson draws to a close, what am I supposed to do? I have to go straight to another lesson for a different kind of getting better and the risk of cognitive overload.

The second camp was mostly from students and parents. Both groups talked about how the slow but undoubtedly steady progression through the math curriculum and the experience of using it was uninspiring and demotivating for everyone, particularly for students who had some aptitude for math.

But it is often small scale, meaning that it is both based on small sample sizes and not always combined to create large scale chunks of data that can be pulled and stretched in different ways. This means that the individual pieces of evidence are often unreliable or invalid to everyone other than the sample from which conclusions were drawn.

These programmes have their downsides; of course they do, especially when teachers report too often, causing themselves and parents cognitive and time overload. On the other hand, I have seen the impact that well-implemented versions of these programmes (start small, get feedback, find out what is helpful and not, reset and aim slightly differently) can have on parents, children and teachers.
